READING

**The core problem restated**

At peak, Fennerbrake needs 72 pallet spaces (18 pallets/day × 4 days between collections). The pro-rata entitlement at Wildern Cross is 52 spaces. The shortfall is 20 spaces. In July 2026 that shortfall cost £45,136 in downgraded fruit, and it will recur every July until something changes.

---

**Course TREGOWAN – working the numbers**

30 additional spaces at Ilsington Chilled covers the gap and leaves 10 in hand (52 + 30 = 82 spaces). Annual out-of-pocket cost: £24,000 rent + £7,200 haulage = **£31,200/year**, payable every season indefinitely. No capital leaves Fennerbrake's account.

Compressor exposure stays at 25% of £260,000 = **£65,000** within three years.

Three-year cash out under TREGOWAN: £93,600 rental + £65,000 compressor = **£158,600**, plus the contention at Wildern Cross remains structurally unchanged.

The buyer query is not a footnote. Soft fruit is among the most handling-sensitive produce that moves through retail supply chains; extra transhipment fourteen miles away, after picking, is a legitimate quality objection. If the buyer applies even a small discount to the full-season volume, or reduces orders, the £31,200 annual saving overstates what TREGOWAN actually saves. The query has already been raised; it will not go away.

---

**Course HAVERSHOLT – working the numbers**

Purchase cost: £96,000. Capital remaining: £140,000 − £96,000 = **£44,000**.

Resulting entitlement: 50% of 208 = **104 spaces** — 32 more than the 72 required, all at Wildern Cross, no split-site handling.

Compressor exposure doubles to 50% of £260,000 = **£130,000** within three years. With £44,000 in reserve after the acquisition, the compressor leaves an **£86,000 gap** that must come from operations over roughly three years.

Three-year cash out under HAVERSHOLT: £96,000 acquisition + £130,000 compressor = **£226,000** in capital, but no rental.

Incremental capital cost of HAVERSHOLT over TREGOWAN: £96,000 (acquisition) + £65,000 (extra compressor exposure) = **£161,000**, offset by £31,200/year not paid to Ilsington. Simple payback on that incremental outlay: **5.2 years**. That is a reasonable return on a long-life capital asset, and the store ownership sits on the balance sheet rather than disappearing as rent.

The 50% shareholding also confers **veto power** over the compressor decision and any future store changes. Under TREGOWAN, Ardwick would hold 75% if they exercise pre-emption and would control the store entirely; Fennerbrake would be a 25% minority with an external rented overflow.

---

**The Ardwick pre-emption risk**

Ardwick's exercising pre-emption would cost them £96,000 plus an increase in compressor exposure from £130,000 (their current 50%) to £195,000 (75%) — a further £65,000 — in order to move from majority control they already effectively exercise to a 75% holding they do not obviously need. The financial incentive to exercise is weak. That said, the risk is real.

Crucially, the timelines interlock: if Fennerbrake makes the offer in September or October 2026, Ardwick's thirty-day window expires before end of November, well inside the 2026-11-30 deadline. If Ardwick exercises pre-emption, Fennerbrake is back at square one by December 2026 and still has until 2027-03-31 to book TREGOWAN. The Ilsington fallback is not foreclosed. Pursuing HAVERSHOLT does not burn the alternative.

---

**The operational funding question**

The £86,000 compressor gap (£130,000 due − £44,000 cash remaining) must come from three seasons of trading. At 14 acres of everbearer strawberries and 6 acres of raspberry under tunnels, with fruit selling at £3.10/kg, peak-season revenue is substantial. The gap is material but not extraordinary for a business of this scale: roughly £29,000/year over three years, roughly equivalent to what TREGOWAN's rental alone would have cost. The annual saving of £31,200 in avoided Ilsington rent substantially offsets the compressor instalments.

---

**The decisive comparison**

| | TREGOWAN | HAVERSHOLT |
|---|---|---|
| Peak spaces | 82 (52 + 30) | 104 |
| Extra handling | Yes – buyer has queried | None |
| Annual rental cost | £31,200 forever | £0 |
| Three-year compressor liability | £65,000 | £130,000 |
| Structural ownership position | Unchanged (25%) | 50%, veto rights |
| Capital tied up | £0 | £96,000 |
| Store voting power | 25% minority | Equal partner |

TREGOWAN is cheaper in the short term and requires no capital. But it rents capacity in a facility fourteen miles away, at a cost the buyer has already flagged as a quality concern, leaves the ownership structure at Wildern Cross exactly as it is, and commits £31,200/year in perpetuity with nothing to show for it.

HAVERSHOLT costs more over three years, tightens capital, and depends on Ardwick not exercising pre-emption. But it permanently solves the chilling shortfall on-site, buys a real asset with lasting value, eliminates recurring rental, confers meaningful governance rights over the store's future, and removes the commercial risk that a quality-conscious buyer has already put on record.

---

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  TREGOWAN's extra off-site handling has already drawn a buyer query that threatens the retail price on the entire crop, and that risk — not the £31,200 annual rental — is what makes HAVERSHOLT's permanent on-site solution and lasting store ownership the clearly preferable course.
